what_this_is: Category names taken out of the full texts of the taxonomy papers, with no seed list. The patterns describe what a category name looks like and where in a paper one stands; they name no category, no criterion and none of the Czech scorer's six.
why_full_texts: A taxonomy lives in a table or a numbered list in the body. Two passes over abstracts returned the few property words that happen to appear in prose, and said so: that was a measurement of where taxonomies are printed, not of what is in them.
the_signal_is_document_frequency: A name one paper invented is a lead. A name several unrelated papers use is the field agreeing that a text has that property, which is what a catalog can be held against. Only names appearing in two or more papers are reported.
no_mapping_here: Which of these the 36 candidates already cover is a judgement, made and recorded in a separate step. A mapping done inside this script would let a new property be talked away where nobody could see it.

extraction.why_not_capitalisation: the first version looked for Title Case near a word about taxonomies and returned `this`, `there`, `while`, `canada` and `vancouver`. Capitalisation cannot tell a category name from the first word of a sentence, so the shape of a printed taxonomy entry replaced it: a label, a colon, a definition.
extraction.header_and_references_are_cut: affiliations gave `dublin` and `ireland`, the bibliography gave `zhang` and `long papers`
extraction.dehyphenation: a two-column PDF breaks words across lines, so 'Con-\ntent Omission' is rejoined before anything else; without it the field's most agreed category is invisible
extraction.stoplist_is_a_declared_bias: every entry is about a document or a study, never a property a text can have

limitations: A table pdftotext scrambles contributes nothing, so this under-reports. A name is not a definition: what each category means still has to be read, and the quote recorded, before it can support a criterion.
outcome: This did not work, and the reason is worth keeping. It returns almost nothing, because a taxonomy is printed as a table or a figure and pdftotext turns both into a bare sequence of words with no label-colon-definition shape left in them. The result is a measurement of how taxonomies are typeset, not of what is in them. Three successive versions of the patterns made it worse rather than better: capitalisation could not tell a category name from the first word of a sentence, and loosening the anchors let the bibliography back in. The categories were read out of the papers by hand instead, with every quote machine-checked against the text file it is attributed to, which is what map_consensus_taxonomy.py records. Kept rather than deleted because the next person to think of mining these PDFs should see that it was tried and what it cost.
